title: Brigid of Kildare
hookLine: abbess and legend-maker; her cross is woven from rushes

cards: A handful of green rushes, pulled from a riverbank. Fold one over another, turn, fold again, and a small square grows in the middle with four arms reaching out.
In Ireland people still make these and hang them over the door or in the kitchen, where they stay until the next one replaces them. It's called Brigid's cross.
The woman it's named for ran a great double community of nuns and monks in Ireland, and so many stories gathered around her that it's hard to see where the woman ends and the legend begins.

teach.b: Start with an early life of her, written by a monk of Kildare named Cogitosus. He says plainly that he's writing down what he heard from older people, so from the first page we're in the land of memory, not records.
Cogitosus tells of a woman whose hands were always open.
She gave food and clothing away so often that, in his telling, what she gave kept coming back: butter that didn't run out, milk that stretched to feed more guests than it should have.
Coming in from the rain, she hung her wet cloak on a beam of sunlight, mistaking it for a wooden beam, and it hung there drying, as if on a peg. Next, the work.
Cogitosus describes Kildare as a large community where both women and men lived under her care, with a church, and people coming from all over for help.
As its abbess, Brigid led it so well that it became a place people traveled toward. Now the cross. It isn't in Cogitosus.
It comes from a later story people tell: Brigid sitting beside a dying man who did not know Christ, picking up rushes from the floor, and weaving a cross while she told him who Jesus was.
In the story, he asks to be baptized before he dies. Some tellings make the man her father, some a chieftain.
Whatever happened by that bed, the cross outlived it. Rushes are about the plainest thing a person could pick up. She used what was on the floor.
Catholics honor Brigid as a saint, one of Ireland's patrons alongside Patrick, and on her feast people still weave her cross.

how: Catholics in Ireland and beyond keep the feast of Saint Brigid, and some families weave a Brigid's cross from rushes or straw to hang over a door or in the kitchen through the year.

games.q: you're Brigid, beside a dying man who has asked who Christ is. there's no book, no chapel, only rushes on the floor. what do you do?
o: send for a priest and wait.

games.why: in the story people tell, she wove a cross from the rushes on the floor as she spoke, and he asked to be baptized.

practice: Lay two plain things across each other, two pens or two twigs; you don't need rushes or a pattern. Hold it in your palm and notice how little it took.
If you pray, hold it while you pray for someone in your home, as people do with Brigid's cross by the door; if not, notice what you made from what was lying around.

wordCard.voice: Brigid. The abbess of Kildare, honored as a saint, remembered for open hands and the cross woven from rushes. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a cross from rushes. Small, plain things can carry a lot. See you tomorrow.
